items.title: A perfect storm is descending on the AI industry
items.summary:
An aerial view of a 33 megawatt data center with closed-loop cooling system on April 14, 2026 in Vernon, California. | Mario Tama/Getty Images 

The stock market is set to christen a new trillion-dollar company on Wednesday, as the AI juggernaut Anthropic goes public.

Key takeaways 

Fears of an AI market crash are growing, with tech stocks sliding sharply since June.

The AI industry is spending far more on infrastructure than it earns, and cheaper “good enough” models threaten the profits of frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.

Three recent shocks have made things worse.

The boom may survive, but AI companies can no longer count on governments deferring to them or markets cheering them on. 

The IPO should have been the crowning triumph of the AI boom — a testament to the technology’s mind-bending commercial value, which enabled a seven-person startup to become a world-conquering juggernaut in five short years.

But all is not well with Silicon Valley. Even as investors scramble to claim a piece of our future God-emperor, Claude Opus 5,000 ( hallowed be his name! ), fears of an AI market crash are building. 

Since June, tech stocks have taken a beating, with one generative AI ETF shedding 35 percent of its value. Over the same period, the Philadelphia semiconductor index — a rough gauge of the chip industry’s value — fell by more than one-third.

The sell-off gained steam in recent weeks, as Republicans lost key elections to AI-skeptical Democrats — and Nvidia lost its longtime CEO to a geopolitically explosive sex scandal, a leadership change that has…

items.title: Xi-Trump-Putin summit: when great powers want to call all the shots, what does it mean for everyone else?
items.summary:
Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump are meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.

The meeting is no doubt unusual – a very rare opportunity for the leaders of the world’s three major powers to exchange views directly on major global issues.

It’s drawn comparisons to the Yalta conference of 1945, when US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian leader Joseph Stalin met to divide the world into spheres of influence after the second world war.

But this is no Yalta 2.0. Nor is the Shenzhen summit an isolated episode. In May this year, Xi hosted back-to-back visits by Trump and Putin to Beijing. Trump reciprocated by hosting Xi in Washington in September, and met with Putin in Alaska last year.

Taken together, these developments signal a broader shift away from the post-Cold War emphasis on global institutions and multilateral consultations toward a more personalised form of great power management.

items.title: When do we start worrying about all these outages?
items.summary:
Have you tried to take a flight in the last week? What about check your email , your bank balance , your Apple account ? (Or, for a select few of us, your top-secret internal spy agency network ?)

If you have, you might have noticed that some or all of those services didn’t work as expected. First, Microsoft’s cloud programs, such as Outlook, went down late last week. Then, all of the planes were grounded on Friday. And this week, we had to deal with the bank outages, a separate United Airlines-specific outage, the Apple outage, and the NSA communications outage. 

As of this writing, most of these issues have now been ironed out, at least for the time being, and there’s no indication that any of them were cyberattacks or otherwise malicious. But whatever the reasons, it sure feels like there have been a lot more outages this week and last than in a usual seven-day stretch. 

To get to the bottom of it — hopefully before something else shorts out — the Today, Explained team spoke with Lily Hay Newman , a senior writer at WIRED who covers hacking, information security, and digital privacy. 

She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about why it took Microsoft so long to get Outlook back on its feet, all of the other recent outages we’ve suffered, and whether it’s as unprecedented as it feels in the moment. Plus, she explains how AI is causing a broader “vulnepocalypse” (or “ Vulnageddon ”), even if it’s not specifically the culprit of all of our current outages.

items.title: Voyager 1 is about to reach a mind-bending milestone
items.summary:
An artist’s rendering of the Voyager approaching Saturn, circa the late 1970s. | Space Fronteirs/Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

Shortly after 5 am ET tomorrow morning, while much of the East Coast is still in bed, Voyager 1 will cross a threshold that’s kind of hard to comprehend.

The 49-year-old spacecraft will reach a point about 16 billion miles from Earth — the distance that light travels in 24 hours. 

Scientists call that unit a light-day. And while it’s not a particularly meaningful scientific measurement, it’s a pretty good opportunity to marvel at how far Voyager has voyaged.

The craft first set out in 1977 to explore our solar system’s outer planets, including Jupiter and Saturn. It flew past both planets, snapping photos of their surfaces and making several big discoveries , before reaching interstellar space in 2012. 

Today, both Voyager and its sister, Voyager 2, remain part of an active NASA mission measuring the gases and magnetic field outside the Sun’s protective magnetic bubble. Both spacecraft also famously carry identical copies of the so-called Golden Record, which contains images and recordings meant to introduce humanity to passing aliens. That means Voyager isn’t just interesting as a live experiment or a souvenir of America’s 1970s space ambitions — but as an attempted self-portrait of human civilization.

items.title: How to be a good-enough home cook
items.summary:
Editor’s note, November 17, 2026, 5 pm ET : This story is being republished for the holiday season. It was originally published in 2022. 

The running gag among anyone who’s ever tasted a morsel of my cooking is that I must not know what salt is. It’s a fair critique: I somehow manage to overcook and under-season virtually every meal I prepare. I’m clumsy and unconfident with a knife and prefer to prepare most foods in a microwave or Instant Pot. 

Whipping up a meal is sometimes a nutritional puzzle. If all you’re working with at the moment are tortillas, frozen broccoli, and canned beans, you (like me) may struggle to conjure up something decent to eat. 

Cooking can also feel like a chore. Parents not only have to feed themselves, but send their kids off to school with packed lunches and prepare snacks and dinner after that. One recipe can dirty up a whole sink’s worth of dishes. 

Just like any other life skill , cooking is one that requires practice. “Eating is such a human thing — that’s the first skill we learn,” says Jess Dang , the founder of the online meal planning service Cook Smarts . “People think if I know how to eat, I must be able to know how to cook too, but they’re totally separate things.” If you weren’t taught the basics of cooking from school or a loved one, you might feel your time in the kitchen is doomed; if you’re already stretched thin financially and time-wise, cooking can feel like a fraught endeavor. However, with a few foundational skills and pantry staples, even the most beginner home chefs can whip up some delicious meals in no time at all.…
items.t: How to be a good-enough home cook

items.title: How Friendsgiving eclipsed Turkey Day
items.summary:
Editor’s note, November 17, 2026, 5 pm ET : This story is being republished for the holiday season. It was originally published in 2018. 

Sara Reinis, a 26-year-old creative strategist at Vox Media, held her first Friendsgiving last year at her apartment in Brooklyn. Between 30 and 40 people showed up to the potluck, multiple of whom brought dishes from the Whole Foods hot bar. The centerpiece? A cake with icing that read, “Gobble gobble, bitch.”

“On the spectrum of ‘typical house party’ to ‘formal Thanksgiving’ it was like, right in the middle,” she says. “The mood was, ‘What if instead of Tostitos, people brought mashed potatoes and pies?’”

The evening was a success, clearly — while some people stayed to help clean up, others went out dancing, and Sara even ended up with a collection of new dishware that people neglected to pick up.

“It can be very rare in New York to get together and eat home-cooked food,” she adds. “So it felt very intimate and cozy the whole evening — even though it was pretty crowded and rowdy at times.”

This weekend, parties like Sara’s will be happening countrywide. Over the past half-decade or so, the week before Thanksgiving has been widely understood as a glorious reprieve before the obligations of actual Thanksgiving, which can range from multi-hour cross-country flights to having to explain who Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is to your great-uncle. By contrast, Friendsgiving season is a time to just hang out with your usual crew and eat slightly more autumnal food than normal.

While the concept of celebrating Thanksgiving with friends isn’t…
items.t: How Friendsgiving eclipsed Turkey Day

items.title: Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone

It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: The US has officially lost control of measles
items.summary:
A healthcare worker takes down signs at a Maryland vaccine clinic. | ﻿Sarah L. Voisin/The Washington Post via Getty Images 

This year, the United States has recorded more measles cases — 5,739 as of Tuesday, November 17 — than in the past 25 years combined. There are active outbreaks in New York , Pennsylvania , and across the Midwest . At least eight people have died with measles infections in the US.

None of this is supposed to happen in the 21st century. In 2000, the United States declared that measles had been eliminated. For years, the extremely rare cases the US saw were from people who contracted the virus in another country and brought it back to America; we didn’t have to worry about measles spreading naturally in our communities.

But that’s no longer true. The Pan American Health Organization, which works with the countries in the Western Hemisphere on ongoing public health threats as well as emergency response, made it official Monday after the annual meeting of its measles and rubella elimination commission: The United States’ measles elimination status has been revoked. The virus is once again endemic in America.

It is an international embarrassment for a country that until very recently was the world’s unquestioned global health leader. And for doctors here in the US who have been practicing for decades, it’s an almost-unthinkable development, putting American lives needlessly at risk. The death of a 7-month-old baby in New York state , who was too young to be vaccinated, has made the consequences of the country’s collective failure hauntingly clear.…
items.t: The US has officially lost control of measles

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.

items.title: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era
items.summary:
James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

items.title: The secret of the new Southern Democrats: They’re super liberal
items.summary:
Sens.-elect Annie Andrews (D-SC) and James Talarico (D-TX) walk through the US Capitol as they arrive for new member orientation meetings for the 120th Congress, in Washington, DC, on November 9, 2026. | Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images 

If you want to own a gun, there are few places better to do it than South Carolina. As the gun rights organization the National Rifle Association (NRA) notes on its database of state gun laws , the Palmetto State has no restrictions on the class of guns dubbed assault weapons or large-capacity magazines; there is no permit required to openly carry firearms. 

Its outgoing governor, Republican Henry McMaster, was supported by the NRA’s political wing, which noted that he netted an “A” rating in their 2018 scores. None of this is surprising. It’s located in the Deep South, after all — that’s the headquarters of America’s gun culture .

But what is surprising is that the NRA lost a key election this midterms, when its candidate , the incumbent Republican Sen. Darline Graham, lost to Democratic nominee Annie Andrews.

“I hate the NRA,” Andrews wrote on her X page in September 2024. In another previous missive, she blamed the NRA for creating a “ hellscape ” at her child’s school where a police officer stands guard during recess. 

The pediatrician-turned-senator-elect was not shy about her view on America’s easy access to guns. She had previously held a job at Everytown for Gun Safety, a group that organizes for more strict gun laws. Her campaign website this cycle included a call to ban “weapons of war from our streets” — an allusion to…
items.t: Meet the new Southern progressives

items.title: Trump closes an AI loophole
items.summary:
President Donald Trump departs the White House on November 16, 2026, ahead of a trip to China and the Philippines. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images 

This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .

Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is closing a global AI chip loophole that the Jensen Huang scandal put in the spotlight.

What’s changing? The Commerce Department is trying to make it harder for China to access top-of-the-line AI microchips like those made by Nvidia.

Currently, China is able to dodge export rules by renting computing power from third-country data centers, which can legally buy American-made chips that China can’t.

But under the rule issued Monday, which is set to take effect in 90 days, data centers in a handful of countries will face new export restrictions on chips — including a requirement that they perform “robust due diligence on their customers” to make sure that they aren’t evading an export ban. 

What’s the context? Huang, who resigned from Nvidia last week, was brought down in part by his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an alleged Chinese spy ( kind of ) and an executive at a Singapore-based tech company, Megaspeed, that was renting compute to Chinese firms — exactly the kind of thing that the new rule aims to crack down on. 

What’s the big picture? The Nvidia scandal is front and center. But under the hood, there’s also some Trump administration infighting going on. As a statement…
items.t: Trump closes an AI loophole

items.title: How to actually fix America’s air traffic control system
items.summary:
What happened on Friday was only the latest symptom of an aging air traffic control system. | Adam Gray/Getty Images 

On Friday evening, in the midst of the second-longest closure ever of US airspace, I bought two plane tickets and found myself contemplating, possibly for the first time, the list of hidden fees tacked onto my fare. 

I had forked over $16.95 for a US transportation tax, plus $5.30 for a flight segment tax, both of which pool into the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, which will ultimately contribute to the Federal Aviation Administration’s work, thereby ensuring that my flight from New York to Florida lands smoothly. 

But though one might expect my $22.25 — enough to pay an air traffic trainee’s salary for about an hour — would go directly into the FAA’s coffers, it does not. In fact, the FAA needs to get congressional approval every time it taps into its trust fund, a political bottleneck that has for decades kept the FAA from making the critical long-term modernization projects it needs to make sure that a single botched cable job is not enough to bring down the busiest airspace in the world.

In the days since all air travel shut down across the United States, we’ve learned a great deal about what happened and why. But the best response to the crisis — and the path to preventing it from happening again (and again and again) — may well be found in shortening the path that my $22.25 takes on its way to the beleaguered agency that needs it so badly. It’s a solution that transformed air travel in Canada — which turned its air traffic control system around…
items.t: How to actually fix America’s air traffic control system

items.title: Damaging the lifeline that Samaritans offers the public | Letters
items.summary:
Volunteers despair as the charity sets about closing local branches and restructuring

Samaritans old and new will, I’m sure, have been just as shocked as I was by your article (‘Is anyone up for a fight?’: The battle for the soul of Samaritans, 10 November). Many, though, will not be surprised. I was a volunteer for 26 years in three branches. The work was demanding and life-changing; the experience is so transformative that it gives every part of society people who are strong enough to bear others’ burdens and able to share their pain. We don’t stop being listeners when we stop being volunteers.

During my time, I found that the people at the top were detached from what went on at branch level. It is not news to me that they cannot understand how central to the work each local branch is and how important every human contact is to those who need to talk.

items.title: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop
items.summary:
On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia.

Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia.

The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices.

Regional flavour

Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together).

While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English.

By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual.

items.t: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop

items.title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
items.summary:
Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked

The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “reactive and risk-averse” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?”

This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. items.title: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
items.summary:
When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so…
items.t: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
